activities.anchor: Every solid is held together by some mix
activities.caption: pair each bond with the property bundle it buys
activities.name: atcBondMatch

config.prompt: Four interactions, four property bundles — pair them:

pairs.right: a movable electron sea — conducts, and lets planes slide, so it dents
electrons transferred — hard, high-melting, and it shatters rather than dents
shared along specific directions — the stiffest materials known, and a poor conductor
flickering attractions — feeble alone, but the glue between chains and sheets

config.why: Bonding type sets the ceiling: every entry in the property tables traces back to which of these four holds the solid together.

activities.anchor: They are among the strongest bonds in the table
activities.caption: call the melting point before you dismiss the bond
activities.name: atcSaltEstimate

config.prompt: If ionic bonds really were weak, rock salt would melt low. Roughly what temperature does it melt at?
config.why: 801 °C — the bonds are strong. The brittleness is geometric: shear the planes by one ion spacing and like charges are brought face to face, and the repulsion cracks the crystal.
config.context: Copper dents because its electron sea forgives any slide; a salt's charges do not.

activities.caption: file each metal by its lattice
activities.name: atcLatticeBuckets

config.prompt: Three lattices take nearly all the metals — file each resident:
config.why: FCC and HCP pack at 74%, BCC sits looser at 68% with coordination 8 — and the packing foretells the mechanics.

config.prompt: The FCC packing fraction, step by step — drag the derivation into order:
items: Atoms touch along the face diagonal: 4r = a√2
So the cell edge is a = 2√2·r
The cell holds 4 whole atoms (8 corners × ⅛ + 6 faces × ½), volume 16πr³/3
config.why: 74% is a mathematical limit — no arrangement of equal spheres beats it (proved only in 2017). Grocers stacking oranges had known it for centuries.

activities.anchor: the famous Liberty ships of WWII
activities.caption: walk the lattice decision
activities.name: atcHullBranch

config.root: It is 1942. You are specifying steel plate for a hull that will serve in the North Atlantic.

start.text: Two candidate steels match on strength and cost at room temperature. Which do you put in the hull?

choices.label: Steel rated to stay ductile at low temperature
choices.feedback: The choice that keeps ships afloat.

bcc.text: BCC iron turns brittle below its ductile-to-brittle transition temperature. In cold water the hull stops denting and starts splitting — the ships that cracked in half were BCC steel below their transition.

choices.label: Re-specify the plate
choices.feedback: One line of crystallography, read in advance, is a safety briefing.

safe.text: The right lattice keeps its slip systems working as the temperature drops: planes keep sliding, the hull dents instead of fracturing. FCC metals carry 12 independent slip systems; HCP metals have few, and fail along certain directions.

config.why: The lattice choice foretells the mechanics — slip systems are the difference between a dent and a crack.

activities.anchor: cooling fast enough to outrun crystallisation
activities.caption: fill the blanks — each level of order has a job
activities.name: atcOrderCloze

config.text: Semiconductor wafers must be %%0%%, because a grain boundary across a transistor is a %%1%% — and jet turbine blades are grown as single crystals by %%2%%, because creep happens at grain boundaries.
config.hint: Two blanks name the failure being designed against; the third names the growth route that beats it.

activities.anchor: Same steel, finer grains, stronger part
activities.caption: which curve is Hall–Petch?
activities.name: atcHallPetchTrace

config.prompt: Yield strength plotted against grain size d — which curve is the Hall–Petch trend?
config.why: Strength rises as one over √d — a dislocation meets more boundaries as grains shrink. (Shrink below ~10–15 nm and the trend itself reverses.)

activities.anchor: domain of validity stamped into it
activities.caption: one line of the strength note overshoots
activities.name: atcHallPetchSpot

config.prompt: A design note on grain refinement — one line is wrong. Click it:
lines: Refine a metal's grains and it gets stronger — the classic trend.
Below roughly 10–15 nm the trend turns around.
There, the boundaries themselves begin to slide, and become the weakness.
So strength rises without limit as grains get ever smaller.
The strongest grains sit at an intermediate size, not the finest.
config.correction: Below ~10–15 nm, grain-boundary sliding takes over as the deformation mechanism — the boundaries that were obstacles become the weakness, and strength peaks at an intermediate size.
config.why: Every design rule has a domain of validity: neither coarse nor ultrafine wins outright.
